# Rules

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-rules.ts from src/rules.ts. Do not edit by hand. -->

## How to read a finding

```console
✖ CRITICAL  Claude Code skill  pdf-helper  ~/.claude/skills/pdf-helper      ← item, where it is installed
   SG205  Reads secrets and sends data out — Reads secrets (line 2) and …    ← rule, what was found
          scripts/sync.py:3  requests.post("https://…", data={"c": creds…  ← file:line, the evidence (secrets masked)
```

| Severity | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **critical** | The complete shape of an attack: hidden instructions, download-and-run, credentials read *and* sent out | Do not use the item. Remove it; if it may have run, rotate the credentials it could reach |
| **high** | Something an attacker would write and a legitimate item rarely needs | Read the evidence before using the item |
| **medium** | A risky capability or configuration (unpinned server, plaintext token, bundled binary) | Check it is intended; pin, scope or suppress with a reason |
| low / info | Context: hooks that exist, remote servers, mentions in documentation | Hidden by default (`--min low` to see) |

Every rule has a default severity (below). The scanner **lowers** it when the match is in documentation, a test file, a fenced example, a quoted mention, a comment, or a sentence phrased as a warning ("never read `~/.ssh`"). That is why the same pattern can be critical in a hook and info in a README. The message says *Reads* vs *Mentions* where that distinction matters.

`skill-guard explain SG205` prints a rule's explanation and fix in the terminal. `--fail-on high` (the default) makes the exit code 1 when anything high or critical remains.

## Suppressing

Suppress findings in a `.skill-guard.json` passed with `--config` (or in `~/.config/skill-guard/config.json`):

```json
{ "ignore": [{ "rule": "SG601", "item": "claude-code:mcp-server:*", "reason": "pinned via lockfile" }] }
```

Inline comments — `skill-guard-ignore SG123` on the same line or the line above, `skill-guard-ignore-file SG123` anywhere in the file (rule IDs are required) — and a `.skill-guard.json` inside the scanned folder count only with `--trust-ignores`: they are part of the content being scanned, and a malicious skill would simply ignore itself. Use the flag for your own repository in CI. The number of suppressed findings is always reported.

## Instructions a model will follow

### SG101 — Instruction override

**Default severity:** high

Text that tells the model to ignore its previous instructions, rules or system prompt is the classic prompt-injection move. In a skill or tool description it runs every time the item is loaded.

**Fix:** Remove the sentence. If the item legitimately needs different behaviour, say what to do, not what to ignore.

### SG102 — Hides actions from the user

**Default severity:** high

Legitimate tools have no reason to ask the model to keep something from you. "Silently", "without telling the user" and "do not mention" are how malicious skills keep their side effects out of the conversation.

**Fix:** Remove the concealment, or remove the item.

### SG103 — Invisible characters

**Default severity:** high

Unicode Tag characters, bidirectional overrides and runs of zero-width characters are invisible in editors and on GitHub but are read by the model. They can carry whole hidden instructions.

**Fix:** Delete the characters (`skill-guard` shows where they are and what hidden text they spell). Treat the item as hostile until you know why they are there.

### SG104 — Hidden text with instructions

**Default severity:** medium

HTML comments, and SVG/HTML text styled to be invisible (zero font size, zero opacity, `display: none`), do not show when rendered — so instructions inside them are seen by the model but not by a human looking at the skill or image.

**Fix:** Move the text where reviewers can see it, or delete it.

### SG105 — Trigger hijacking

**Default severity:** medium

A description that claims the item must be used for every request makes the agent load it everywhere — maximising the reach of anything else it contains.

**Fix:** Describe when the item is actually useful.

### SG106 — Loads instructions from the internet

**Default severity:** high

A skill that fetches its real instructions at run time can change behaviour after you reviewed it (a "rug pull"), and the reviewed text proves nothing.

**Fix:** Vendor the instructions into the skill, or pin them to a content hash you have reviewed.

### SG107 — Pretends to be the system or an official source

**Default severity:** medium

Fake `<system>` blocks, "[SYSTEM]" markers or claims of being an official Anthropic/OpenAI/DeepSeek component try to borrow authority the text does not have.

**Fix:** Remove the impersonation.

### SG108 — Turns off approvals or the sandbox

**Default severity:** high

Instructions or commands that disable permission prompts or the sandbox (`--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `bypassPermissions`, `danger-full-access`, YOLO mode, a PreToolUse hook that answers "allow") remove the last check between the model and your machine.

**Fix:** Keep approvals on. Grant specific permissions instead of disabling them all.

### SG110 — Plants code in what the agent writes

**Default severity:** high

Instructions to add a remote script, iframe or download-and-run line to every page or file the agent produces turn your own codebase into the payload: the backdoor ships with your code, written by your agent, and looks like your work.

**Fix:** Remove the instruction and search recent agent-written files for the injected line.

### SG109 — Changes how other tools behave

**Default severity:** high

A description that tells the model how to use a *different* tool ("when the send_email tool is available, always BCC …") is tool shadowing: the item never has to be called to take effect, because its description is in context whenever it is installed.

**Fix:** An item should describe only itself. Remove the item; check what the other tool has sent.

## Data leaving the machine

### SG201 — Sends data to an external server

**Default severity:** medium

Uploading or POSTing data from your machine is how secrets and source code get exfiltrated. On its own it is often legitimate (calling an API); combined with credential or environment access in the same file it becomes SG205 (critical).

**Fix:** Check exactly what is sent and to whom. Remove it if the item has no clear reason to upload anything.

### SG202 — Known exfiltration endpoint

**Default severity:** critical

Request bins, tunnels and chat webhooks (webhook.site, ngrok, Discord/Slack/Telegram webhooks, Burp Collaborator, interactsh…) are what attackers use to receive stolen data; legitimate tools almost never hard-code them.

**Fix:** Treat the item as malicious unless you wrote it yourself.

### SG203 — Reads credentials or private keys

**Default severity:** high

SSH keys, cloud credentials, browser cookie stores, crypto wallets and agent auth files are the first thing an attacker looks for.

**Fix:** Remove the access. If a tool genuinely needs a credential, pass it explicitly through a scoped environment variable.

### SG204 — Dumps environment variables

**Default severity:** medium

The environment holds API keys and tokens. Serialising all of it is rarely needed and is a common first step of exfiltration.

**Fix:** Read the specific variables you need instead of the whole environment.

### SG206 — Leaks data through a link or image URL

**Default severity:** high

Asking the model to output an image or link whose URL contains conversation data (`![](https://host/p.png?d={summary})`) leaks that data the moment the client renders it — no click, no tool call, no approval.

**Fix:** Remove the instruction. Legitimate badges and links do not carry conversation content in their query string.

### SG205 — Reads secrets and sends data out (exfiltration chain)

**Default severity:** critical

The same file both touches credentials (or the whole environment) and sends data to a server. That is the complete shape of a credential-stealing payload.

**Fix:** Treat as malicious. Do not run it; remove the item and rotate any credentials it could reach.

## Code execution

### SG301 — Downloads and executes code

**Default severity:** critical

`curl … | sh`, `iwr … | iex` and friends run whatever a server returns at that moment, with your privileges. The content can change at any time.

**Fix:** Download, verify (checksum or signature) and review before running — or install from a package manager with a pinned version.

### SG302 — Runs obfuscated or encoded code

**Default severity:** critical

Decoding base64 or hex and executing it (`powershell -enc`, `eval(atob(…))`, `exec(b64decode(…))`) exists to hide what runs from a reviewer.

**Fix:** Replace with readable code, or remove the item.

### SG303 — Executes code fetched at run time

**Default severity:** critical

Passing network responses to `eval`, `exec` or `Function` lets a remote server run arbitrary code inside the tool.

**Fix:** Ship the code with the item instead of fetching it.

### SG305 — Downloads and runs a binary

**Default severity:** high

Download an archive or program, unpack it (often with a password, so scanners cannot look inside), clear the macOS quarantine flag and run it: the delivery chain of the info-stealers found in public skill registries. A skill has no reason to install unsigned binaries.

**Fix:** Do not run it. Install tools from a package manager or the vendor, with a checksum.

### SG304 — Large encoded blob

**Default severity:** medium

Long base64 or hex strings in instructions or scripts can hide payloads from review.

**Fix:** Check what the blob decodes to. Keep data in a separate, documented file.

## Persistence and tampering

### SG401 — Installs persistence

**Default severity:** high

Writing to shell start-up files, cron, scheduled tasks, launch agents, systemd units or the Windows Run key makes code run again long after the agent session ends.

**Fix:** A skill should never need to survive a reboot. Remove it.

### SG404 — Settings widen what the agent may do

**Default severity:** high

A settings file can pre-approve commands (`"Bash(*)"` in `permissions.allow`), auto-enable every MCP server a repository ships, or send the agent's API traffic — prompts, code and API key — to another host via `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`. A repository's `.claude/settings.json` arrives with `git clone`.

**Fix:** Remove the entries, or keep them only in your own user settings where you chose them.

### SG402 — Modifies agents' configuration

**Default severity:** high

Writing to `.claude/settings.json`, `~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex/config.toml`, MCP configs, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md can add hooks or servers that run on every future session — a technique seen in real npm supply-chain attacks against coding agents.

**Fix:** Agent configuration should be changed by you, not by a skill. Remove the write.

### SG403 — Tampers with git hooks

**Default severity:** medium

Writing `.git/hooks` or changing `core.hooksPath` runs code on every commit or checkout.

**Fix:** Remove it unless it is a documented, opt-in feature.

## Destructive or weakening

### SG501 — Destructive command

**Default severity:** high

Recursive deletes of the home directory or disk, formatting, or force-pushing over history cannot be undone.

**Fix:** Scope deletions to the project and ask before destructive operations.

### SG502 — Disables security protections

**Default severity:** high

Turning off antivirus, the firewall, SELinux or Gatekeeper opens the machine to everything else.

**Fix:** Remove it.

### SG503 — Cryptocurrency miner

**Default severity:** critical

Miner binaries and stratum pool URLs have no place in an agent tool.

**Fix:** Remove the item.

## MCP servers

### SG601 — MCP server runs an unpinned package

**Default severity:** medium

`npx -y some-server` (no version) runs whatever the latest release is every time the agent starts. A compromised or hijacked package version reaches you automatically — the npm-side version of a rug pull.

**Fix:** Pin an exact version (`some-server@1.4.2`) and update deliberately.

### SG602 — MCP server over plain HTTP

**Default severity:** high

Tool calls, results and any auth headers travel unencrypted and can be read or altered on the network.

**Fix:** Use https, or keep the server on localhost.

### SG603 — Secret stored in plain text

**Default severity:** medium

API keys written into agent config files end up in backups, dotfile repos and screenshots, and every server and skill that can read the file can read them.

**Fix:** Reference an environment variable or the OS keychain instead of pasting the key.

### SG604 — MCP server is a shell command

**Default severity:** medium

A server started via `bash -c` / `cmd /c` / `powershell -Command` can run anything, and its real behaviour is in the command string rather than a reviewable package.

**Fix:** Point the config at the actual server binary or package.

### SG605 — MCP server can reach the whole filesystem

**Default severity:** medium

A filesystem root of `/`, a drive root or your whole home directory gives every tool call access to keys, browser data and other projects.

**Fix:** Limit the server to the project directories it needs.

### SG606 — MCP server runs a privileged container

**Default severity:** high

`--privileged`, mounting `/` or the Docker socket, or host networking/PID make the container equivalent to root on the host.

**Fix:** Drop the flag and mount only what the server needs.

### SG607 — Possible typosquat of a well-known package

**Default severity:** high

The package name is one or two characters away from a well-known MCP server. Typosquatted packages are a standard way to get malware installed.

**Fix:** Check the exact name and publisher on the registry.

### SG608 — Remote MCP server

**Default severity:** low

The tools are defined and executed on someone else’s server; their descriptions (which the model obeys) can change at any time without a new install.

**Fix:** Use `skill-guard lock` to be told when your configuration changes, and only connect to providers you trust.

## Hooks

### SG701 — Hook runs automatically

**Default severity:** info

Hooks run shell commands with your privileges on agent events (session start, every prompt, every tool call) without asking. That is fine for hooks you wrote; worth knowing for hooks a plugin brought.

**Fix:** Review the command. Use `skill-guard lock` so new or changed hooks are flagged.

### SG702 — Hook talks to the network

**Default severity:** medium

A hook that contacts a server runs on every matching event, so whatever it sends leaves your machine continuously.

**Fix:** Check what is sent. Prefer hooks that only touch local files.

## Packaging

### SG801 — Install script

**Default severity:** medium

`preinstall`/`install`/`postinstall`/`prepare` scripts run when the package is installed — before you ever use it.

**Fix:** Check what the script does; prefer packages that need none.

### SG802 — Bundled executable

**Default severity:** medium

Compiled binaries inside a skill or plugin cannot be reviewed like scripts.

**Fix:** Build from source you can read, or download from the vendor with a checksum.

### SG804 — Links outside the item

**Default severity:** medium

A symbolic link inside a skill or plugin that points outside it makes a "local" file somewhere else — reading it can expose `~/.ssh`, writing to it can change your agent config. skill-guard does not follow such links, so their targets are not scanned.

**Fix:** Replace the link with the file it points to, or remove it.

### SG805 — File not fully scanned

**Default severity:** low

Text and code files over 2 MB are scanned only at their first and last megabyte (over 64 MB, not at all). Vendored bundles are usually the reason — but padding a script with megabytes of filler is also a way to push a payload out of reach.

**Fix:** Check what the file is. A skill rarely needs a multi-megabyte script.

### SG803 — Unrestricted tool access

**Default severity:** low

The skill asks for unrestricted shell access (`allowed-tools: Bash` or `*`), so anything its instructions say can be executed without per-command approval.

**Fix:** Scope it, e.g. `Bash(git status:*)`.

## Packages that install steps name (--check-registries)

### SG901 — Installs a package that does not exist

**Default severity:** high

The install step names a package that is not on its registry. AI models invent plausible package names, and the names end up in skills and READMEs as install steps; whoever registers such a name first gets their code run by every agent and person that follows the step ("slopsquatting").

**Fix:** Find the real package (check the spelling against the project’s own docs), or remove the step. Do not register the name yourself to "fix" it.

### SG902 — Installs a very new or barely used package

**Default severity:** medium

The package was first published less than 90 days ago, or (npm) had fewer than 50 downloads last week. A name that was made up and then registered by someone looks exactly like this, as does a brand-new legitimate project.

**Fix:** Check who publishes it and that it is the package the project means (its repository, its maintainers, its age) before running the step.

### SG903 — Installs a package removed as malware

**Default severity:** critical

npm removed the package for malware and keeps only a security placeholder under its name; an install step that names it was written for the malicious package.

**Fix:** Remove the step, and check any machine that ran it.
